items.content:
RT @spycraft101: Declassified photos from Polish government archives show methods for breaking into US State Department diplomatic mail pouches during the Cold War.

Diplomatic mail is protected both by international agreements and many different anti-tamper mechanisms, but it also represents a valuable target for any intelligence organization. During the Cold War, the Polish People’s Republic routinely hijacked, exploited, and returned State Department mail, always undetected.

A small team codenamed Typhoon from Department II of the Secret Service was stationed in a secret room at Okecie Airport in Warsaw. When diplomatic pouches arrived, they would be passed through a trap door to the Typhoon team. Seals would be broken, and the internal black plastic bags were destroyed. The contents would be photographed and then the black bags were replaced with exact copies they’d created after extensive examinations of earlier packages. The seals would also be replaced, and the package would be returned to the diplomatic courier, who was none the wiser.

But opening diplomatic pouches was just one part of their operation. Another team formed Section IX, tasked with surreptitiously entering foreign embassies and consulates at night when they were unoccupied. The team didn’t just break in once but regularly entered many of the supposedly secure facilities on a weekly basis, disabling security systems, picking locks, and photographing classified materials.

The key to their success was also their greatest danger: radiation. Section IX built powerful, portable x-ray machines to bombard vault doors and reveal their inner workings. Team members were often exposed to radiation 500x greater than was safe. As a result, many succumbed to cancer later in life.

For episode 122 of the Spycraft 101 podcast I spoke with Tomasz Awlasewicz, author of Invisible. We discussed the methods they refined to access secure rooms in foreign embassies and consulates in Poland, and the heavy price the technicians and operatives of Section IX paid for their groundbreaking work. The episode is available now.

RT @Laughing_Mantis: I would *love* to sit down with everyone who came up with this report.

I was the independent person responsible to do patch analysis for very large companies and facilities for many years. By that I mean I was at one point the single person responsible for pulling the $12+ million dollar switch for several Forbes 100 companies. Matter of fact that's how most of my old school followers know me, I used to dump the work in real time here on Twitter to get more customers (it worked).

So what does that mean?

Patch Tuesday is a great example, it used to drop 10AM PST Tuesday.

I would have an approx 50 page report Friday EoB to customers covering EVERY patch, ease of exploitation, profile the discovery team or person behind it, use in the wild, IoCs, weaponization likelihood in the next 24h, 72h, 7 days, 14 days, 30 days. No AI. Just IDA, DarunGrim, BinDiff, some tools I wrote and a dream. I would be in the office, Tuesday leave Friday, yes, that's correct, no home, straight working. I performed this service from 3 different companies to various customers. Sometimes it was with a select team, most of my career it was solo.

So what was the $12m switch? Well that was the cost it would be for just one of my customers to push out an emergency patch that wasn't in their already accepted patching procedures. That cost was electricity costs, server down time, service availability impact, employee costs, testing etc.

I was the person that said: this patch needs to be pushed and that break glass needs to happen due to impact being greater than X million in a 72h period.

I made that specific call maybe 11 times, in the 14 years that I did this service and I got that call twice. 

The last time I got the call wrong was one of the TCP.sys icmp vulns, ping of death style. I failed to account that another vendors vulnerability would come out to put it to shame and be far more easier to exploit with a PoC.

The other time I got it wrong was exploitation happened about 96h instead of 72h.

The science to get this precision is hard, I got lucky a few times. What I will say is the goal of the attackers, what is at risk, and level of sophistication that attackers will use completely vary from target to target. Also there's a ton of this exploitation data is simply not visible, a lot of this data isn't public and requires lots of embedded resources, sources, and detailed tracking.

In almost all cases and scenarios during those 14 years: 0days are not kings, it's your trash exploits (auth bypass, file upload, hash leaks etc) that are 2 to 6 years old that got forgotten, unpatched, suddenly exposed to the Internet, or bridged over by a contractor that lead to massive incidents over and over.

RT @nextronresearch: A reminder of how cool THOR Thunderstorm and its collectors are ⚡

Some systems will never run a security agent: ESXi hosts, network appliances, routers, industrial and out-of-support systems. They are still part of your attack surface.

The trick: don't bring the scanner to the machine. Bring the machine's files to the scanner.

- A collector (one Go binary, or one script in Bash, POSIX sh, Python, Perl, PowerShell or Batch) copies selected files to your own THOR Thunderstorm. The originals stay where they are.
- You decide what leaves: recent files, a size limit, selected types. Preview it with a dry run first.
- THOR does the heavy lifting on your server: YARA rules, your own signatures, IOCs, Sigma rules and forensic parsers.
- Findings land in a log, in syslog or in your SIEM. Run it every night with cron or Ansible and ship only what changed.

No agent. Often a shell and a network connection are enough.

items.content:
RT @ptdbugs: SMS of Death: Zero-Click Android Telephony DoS via WAP Push

Read on dbugs: https://t.co/GE7F4hH64x

A researcher has published an analysis of a vulnerability in the Android telephony stack that allows an attacker to remotely disable a phone with a single text message. The attack is zero-click: it requires no interaction from the victim and causes a persistent denial of service, including preventing the victim from calling emergency services.

What’s the issue?
The flaw is located in the "WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu()" method in the "frameworks/opt/telephony" system component. The WSP header is parsed as a "uintvar", returned as a "long", then cast to "int" without range checking and used directly as the size of a new array:
│ // https://t.co/YbnrbSPLH2
│ int headerLength = (int) pduDecoder.getValue32();
│ // https://t.co/xLHo5VJITX
│ byte[] header = new byte[headerLength];
The five-byte value "88 80 80 80 00" decodes to "0x80000000". When cast to a signed 32-bit integer, it becomes "-2147483648". Allocating an array with a negative length throws an uncaught "NegativeArraySizeException", crashing the main telephony thread.

Attack mechanics
• Delivery vector. The message is delivered as a data SMS via WAP Push to port 2948. It does not appear in Messages, the sender’s number is not displayed, and no notifications are shown.
• Immediate effect. The "https://t.co/QWrt3u4DYv" process crashes, active calls are dropped, telephony service becomes unavailable for 1–2 seconds, and the process then restarts.
• Carrier redelivery. If the message is not acknowledged, the carrier resends it, causing the phone to crash again. In testing, a single message triggered recurring outages for up to a week.
• Boot loop. The malformed message remains queued in "content://sms/raw" and is reprocessed on every boot. Android RescueParty reboots the device into recovery mode approximately every 90 seconds, eventually prompting the user to perform a factory reset.

Impact on emergency calls
While the device is under attack or stuck in a reboot loop, it cannot reliably place emergency calls. The attack may not only disrupt the phone’s operation but also result in the carrier blocking the device until the issue is resolved. For example, in Australia, access to the 000 emergency number is a mandatory feature of mobile service. Carriers are required to identify phones that cannot connect to emergency services and may disconnect affected devices from the network.

Article: https://t.co/GgEi0S7iIC

🔥 *𝘀𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗲 Checker: Hunting for exposed OpenSSH systems with KQL
​
OpenSSH 𝟭𝟬.𝟲𝗽𝟮 was released on November 5, 2026, with a fix for a newly disclosed password-authentication bypass affecting certain Linux systems running 𝗺𝘂𝘀𝗹 𝗹𝗶𝗯𝗰 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗣𝗔𝗠.
​
The vulnerability, dubbed *𝘀𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗲, 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘀 CVE-2026-123158 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 CVSS v3.1 score of 8.1 (High).
​
⚠️ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
​
Alpine Linux is a notable affected platform. On vulnerable configurations, an attacker who can reach the SSH service may be able to authenticate to an account locked with * in /𝚎𝚝𝚌/𝚜𝚑𝚊𝚍𝚘𝚠 by supplying a password between 𝟮𝟱𝟳 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝟭,𝟬𝟮𝟰 𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝘀. ​
🔎 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲

RT @LoveMHz: After 25 years, the original Xbox's last hidden ROM has finally been dumped: the CPU's microcode!

This has been a goal of mine for over 6 years, and I've worked on it off and on ever since.

Over the last couple of weeks, while building inventory and shipping orders, I've also been running hardware tests 24/7. This poor Xbox has rebooted over 50,000 times in those two weeks alone.

And it finally paid off.

The dump covers the entire 4,096-line microcode address space. The ROM itself occupies 3,200 of those lines, roughly 12 KB of microcode.

I can't overstate how huge this feels. After all these years, I finally have it.

A full write-up is coming next year!
